content: Dysmenorrhoea, commonly referred to as period pain, is a prevalent condition that significantly affects the well-being and productivity of women. Primary dysmenorrhoea is characterized by recurrent, cramping pelvic pain that occurs during menstruation in the absence of any abnormalities in the uterus, ovaries, or fallopian tubes. The underlying cause is believed to be excessive uterine contractions triggered by elevated levels of local chemicals, such as prostaglandins. These prostaglandins stimulate the uterine muscle (myometrium) to contract forcefully, leading to reduced oxygen supply to the tissue and resulting in pain. Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, is widely used in clinical practice to manage preterm labor due to its ability to inhibit uterine contractions. This review aimed to evaluate whether nifedipine could also alleviate uterine contractions and associated pain during menstruation. To assess the effectiveness and safety of nifedipine for primary dysmenorrhoea, a comprehensive search was conducted for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving nifedipine for this condition. The search included both published and unpublished studies, with no language restrictions, and was performed in collaboration with the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group. Databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL were searched up to November 25, 2021. Additional sources included international trial registries, Web of Science, OpenGrey, LILACS, PubMed, and Google Scholar. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. The review included RCTs that compared nifedipine with placebo for the treatment of primary dysmenorrhoea. The primary outcomes assessed were pain relief and health-related quality of life, while secondary outcomes included adverse effects, patient satisfaction, and the need for additional medication. Two independent reviewers evaluated the trials, but the data were insufficient for a meaningful meta-analysis. The evidence reviewed was of very low quality overall. Three small RCTs, involving a total of 106 participants, were identified. Data for analysis were available from only two trials, which included 66 participants. Two of these trials were conducted in the 1980s, and the third in 1993. The findings suggested that nifedipine might be effective for providing any pain relief compared to placebo in women with primary dysmenorrhoea. The odds ratio (OR) for this outcome was 9.04, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 2.61 to 31.31, based on two studies with 66 participants. If the rate of pain relief with placebo is 40%, the rate with nifedipine would be estimated to range between 64% and 95%. For the outcome of good or excellent pain relief, nifedipine appeared to be more effective than placebo, but the confidence interval was very wide (OR 43.78, 95% CI 5.34 to 259.01). The evidence was of very low quality. It was unclear whether nifedipine reduced the need for additional analgesia compared to placebo (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.07 to 4.20, based on one study with 42 participants). Participants expressed a preference for nifedipine over their previous analgesic if it were available. Adverse effects and menstruation-related symptoms were reported at similar levels in both the nifedipine and placebo groups (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.08 to 10.90, based on one study with 24 participants). If the likelihood of adverse effects with placebo is 80%, the rate with nifedipine would be estimated to range between 24% and 98%. No data were available regarding the formal assessment of health-related quality of life. The authors concluded that the evidence is insufficient to confirm whether nifedipine is an effective treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea. The included trials were small and of low quality, with notable imbalances in participant numbers between placebo and treatment groups in one of the two trials with analyzable data. While no significant differences in adverse effects were observed between groups, larger and more rigorously conducted trials are needed to determine the potential role of nifedipine in managing this condition. If proven effective and well-tolerated, nifedipine could be a valuable addition to the therapeutic options for primary dysmenorrhoea. Nifedipine has an established safety profile in women of reproductive age, as demonstrated by its use in preterm labor, and clinicians are familiar with its off-label use for this purpose. The drug is inexpensive and widely available. Current treatment options for primary dysmenorrhoea, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), are not suitable for all women. NSAIDs and OCPs may be contraindicated in some cases, and OCPs are not appropriate for women attempting to conceive. Additionally, the trials reviewed suggest that participants may prefer nifedipine as a treatment option.
